cards.title: Hook objective: qualify viewers, not just grab attention
cards.summary: A hook's job is to pull in relevant users at the right awareness stage so you can educate them, not to indiscriminately capture everyone.
cards.use_when: Writing or auditing the opening 3-5 seconds of a paid social video ad for a product page or direct-response campaign.
steps: Define the objective of the hook as qualifying and pulling in the specific target demographic, not maximizing raw attention.

Reject curiosity gimmicks that attract everyone regardless of product relevance — e.g. stabbing a product with a knife to open a curiosity gap. This grabs indiscriminate viewers and feeds bad optimization data to the Meta targeting algorithm.

Instead use a persona call-out hook that names the exact problem and audience, such as 'GLP-1 hair loss hits hard' or 'Your sauna sessions are burning off your hair.' These immediately filter viewership to the target demographic.
Ask: does the hook make a relevant viewer think 'this is about me' or only 'what is going on?'
Check that the hook's implied awareness stage matches the stage the rest of the ad actually serves.
caveats: Source acknowledges a counter-argument: a visible product on screen (e.g. a protein shaker) might filter viewers by interest — but the presenter doubts this actually happens in practice.
Curiosity hooks can still work as part of a larger qualified message; the problem is curiosity without qualification.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Match the hook's awareness stage to the ad's body stage
cards.summary: A top-of-funnel hook running into a bottom-of-funnel product-tour body creates mismatched data and poor performance.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a video ad has high attention but low conversion on a store's Meta campaign.
steps: Classify the hook's intended audience stage: top-of-funnel curiosity hooks target problem-unaware or broadly problem-aware users; persona hooks target a specific problem-aware segment.
Classify the ad body: listing features and ingredients is bottom-of-funnel, product-aware content; education about the problem and mechanism is upper-funnel.
If the hook is broad and top-of-funnel but the body is a product tour, the hook pulls in people who aren't ready for the pitch and the ad mismatches its own serving stage.
Decide the stage you want to serve (top, middle, bottom) and align both hook and body to that one stage.

The Magic Mind example: a knife-into-product curiosity hook introducing the product by the third word, followed by ingredient and feature education, is a bottom-funnel product ad using a top-funnel hook — the presenter attributes the mismatch to weak performance.
caveats: Presented as the source's analysis of specific examples, not a guaranteed performance rule.
Bottom-of-funnel product ads can perform well with product-aware audiences; the issue is only the mismatch with the hook.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Write a bridge that delays the product pitch
cards.summary: The transition from hook to educational body is the 'bridge', and introducing the product too aggressively or early breaks the educational narrative and builds less trust.
cards.use_when: Restructuring a video ad script where the product pitch arrives too fast after the hook.
steps: Identify the bridge: the transition from the hook into the educational or problem-agitating body of the ad.
Avoid hard-selling the product inside the bridge. Introducing the product immediately after problem agitation feels too aggressive and tends to underperform.

Extend the education by a few lines before the pitch. In the FU2 creatine gummy example, the presenter suggests adding a line about the founder doing due diligence and reaching out to international suppliers before revealing the product.
In the IM8 gut example, the presenter suggests continuing to educate on prebiotics and postbiotics before bridging to 'one supplement instead of several' — an extra four to six seconds of education.
Confirm the bridge explains the mechanism or 'why the product works' before naming it, so viewers arrive at the product with intent rather than being sold to mid-epiphany.
caveats: The source explicitly says these are hypotheses from single examples; brand results are illustrative, not promised.
Delaying too long may lose viewers who are already product-aware and want the offer.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Attack problem-agitation and objection handling, not just features
cards.summary: Sell benefits and resolve the viewer's real objections instead of listing ingredients and materials.
cards.use_when: Writing the body of a video ad or product-page copy where the audience needs to understand why the product works.
steps: Translate every feature into a benefit in the viewer's life — e.g. 'velvet suede material' becomes 'taking a nap at work.'
Agitate the problem against an enemy: in the NAD ad, injections are positioned as painful, expensive and inconvenient, making the oral alternative the obvious conclusion.
Hand a strong objection: the shaker example handles 'I bought a metal one and it was still plastic,' reducing the addressable market but deepening relevance with buyers who experienced that.
Stack social proof and credibility for the solution, e.g. referencing a 12-week clinical trial with reported percentages (85% better digestion and less bloating; 95% more energy).
Check that the benefit still lands for someone who does not do the activity (e.g. creatine benefits for sleep-deprived, brain-health viewers rather than only gym-goers).
caveats: Trial figures in the example are the brand's claimed results and specific to that ad, not general benchmarks.
Objection handling that is too narrow (e.g. 'you bought a plastic metal shaker') can shrink your total addressable market.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Add dynamic editing to prevent drop-off on static talking heads
cards.summary: A long talking-head shot without overlays, B-roll or cuts becomes boring and viewers skip to a reel instead.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or editing a talking-head video ad that is underperforming on hold rate.
steps: Treat lack of movement as a primary drop-off driver; viewers scrolling feeds will skip a static shot in favor of a real.
Add overlays, B-roll and rapid cutting — the source recommends cutting roughly every 3 seconds at minimum.
Add basic motion even without a full edit: the presenter suggests him holding the camera and pulling it in and out.

Compare the creatine gummies ad (heavy overlays and editing, reportedly around 20 times more engaging in the source's assessment) against the shaker ad (good script, static talking head) to see the gap.
Improve the script as well, but recognize that a good script delivered with no motion can still fail.
caveats: The 'cut every 3 seconds' figure is a source recommendation, not a universal benchmark.
'20 times more engaging' is the presenter's subjective comparison of two example ads.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Use a multi-persona call-out to widen the top of funnel
cards.summary: Calling out three related personas instead of one hooks more of the market while still qualifying the audience.
cards.use_when: Writing the opening line of a video ad for a broad-appeal product like a supplement.
steps: Replace a single narrow condition call-out with a list of related conditions. The IM8 example opens with 'You have IBS, leaky gut, or bloating' — hitting three personas at once.
Note that if the ad had said only 'leaky gut', most viewers would have self-excluded.

After the call-out, reinforce that the problem is common and undiagnosed, e.g. '40% of people have it, most don't even know.' This increases the perceived addressable market and viewer self-identification.
If you name a clinical term, immediately explain why the viewer probably has it; the source warns that naming 'dysbiosis' and moving on loses people who don't recognize it.
Keep the call-out language specific to the target demographic so it does not read as generic.
caveats: The 40% figure comes from the example ad's claim, not an independent statistic.
Broadening too far weakens relevance; the source's point is to widen within the product's true market.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Don't shrink TAM with overly narrow brand positioning
cards.summary: Positioning a mass-market supplement toward elite athletes can cap scalability because the addressable market is too small and hard to reach.
cards.use_when: Deciding the target persona and positioning for a supplement or wellness product page and ad messaging.
steps: Estimate the true addressable market before committing to a persona. The source argues the main market for supplements is sedentary people, the majority of the population.
Sell benefits that apply without the gym: sleep deprivation support, brain health, cellular energy and general wellbeing.
Avoid 'not for the everyday sedentary crowd, this is for serious athletes' positioning because it excludes the largest buyer group and makes a large business unlikely.
Account for the operational friction of the elite athlete segment: coaches oversee what athletes take and there are more compliance restrictions.
Verify any health claim you use is compliant; the source itself flags uncertainty on some claims.
caveats: The source's claim about TAM size and scalability is the presenter's opinion, illustrated with a specific Australian creatine brand example.
Compliance rules vary by market; check claims before publishing.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Define niche terms so credentials don't backfire
cards.summary: If you name a technical ingredient or condition, be precise; a knowledgeable audience will catch errors and lose trust.
cards.use_when: Writing product education for a specialized audience where incorrect terminology risks credibility.
steps: Check your ingredient list for redundancy or inaccuracy before publishing. The source points out an ad claiming 'three ingredients: electrolytes, magnesium and creatine' while magnesium is itself an electrolyte.
If the target audience is elite athletes, assume they know the science and will spot the error.
Match vocabulary precision to the audience: the more specialized the persona, the less forgiving the copy.
Apply the same check to disease names and mechanisms — if you say NAD decline causes symptoms, be ready to explain why, or the claim reads as unsupported.
Use plain terms when possible; the presenter notes the NAD ad under-educates on what NAD is and therefore fits solution-aware audiences rather than problem-aware ones.
caveats: The source calls its own critique 'nitpicky' but argues precision still matters to the target audience.
This is a copy-accuracy principle, not a compliance guarantee.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Edit out AI-scripting giveaways, especially contrast negation
cards.summary: The 'it's not X, it's Y' construction is a tell that a script was AI-written and should be avoided or rewritten.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a script drafted by an AI tool before producing a video or writing product page copy.
steps: Scan the script for contrast negation: statements like 'Your gut isn't broken, it's starving' or 'Your gut isn't broken, it's not X, it's Y.'
Add an explicit instruction when prompting AI copywriters: 'Do not use contrast negation.' The source recommends this as a standing rule.
Look for other AI tells noted in the source, such as overused analogies like 'sending a single soldier into a war zone' and hyperbolic scientific framing that reads as generic.
Rewrite the flagged lines into concrete, specific claims that keep the message but sound like a person talking.
Ask whether the line survives a viewer's skeptical ear; the presenter says such lines are a 'huge giveaway' that the ad is AI-scripted.
caveats: This is the presenter's stylistic judgment; some contrast-negation lines may still work in tested ads.
Compliance and tone still need separate review from AI-tell removal.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Leverage a credible figure and a native setting for authenticity
cards.summary: A famous figure shot in a car, paired with trending terms, builds credibility and feels organic rather than like an ad.
cards.use_when: Planning a founder-led or celebrity-led video ad creative for a product or landing-page hero video.
steps: Open with a known figure to borrow general credibility, even when they are not a category expert — the NAD example uses a Transformers actor.
Include a viral or in-demand keyword in on-screen text, e.g. 'peptides' and 'NAD+', to create curiosity for the unfamiliar term.
Shoot in a native, organic-looking setting such as a car rather than a pro studio. The source notes that a three-camera lighting-rig setup immediately signals 'this is an ad.'
Use conversation or interview framing so the hook reads as content rather than a commercial.
Weigh the compliance risk of using a famous person's image and voice; the source flags uncertainty and says the brands doing it seem to manage it.
caveats: Using a public figure's likeness may carry compliance or rights risk — the source is unsure and says to verify.
Celebrity credibility is general, not category-specific; viewers may not see them as an expert on the product.
The source calls the example's script 'sloppy' even though it performed well.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Reinforce relevance after naming a condition
cards.summary: Naming a clinical term is only useful if you immediately convince viewers they likely have it.
cards.use_when: Writing product education about a health problem or a technical product benefit that viewers don't already know they have.
steps: State the condition or mechanism in plain language.
Immediately add prevalence and invisibility framing: '40% of people have it, most don't even know.' This does double duty — market size and self-diagnosis.
Avoid dropping a term like 'dysbiosis' and moving on; the source says viewers will wonder what it means and assume it does not apply to them.
Follow the term with observable symptoms the viewer recognizes so the framework attaches to their experience.
In the IM8 example, the ad then explains the cascade (good bacteria die, bad bacteria take over, inflammation, leaky gut, poor nutrient absorption) before referencing the product.
caveats: Prevalence claims in the example come from the ad itself and were not independently verified.
Health claims and disease references may be regulated; confirm compliance for your market.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Structure a VSL's first 30-40 seconds as hook, problem, mechanism
cards.summary: A long-form video sales letter typically runs 3-4 minutes; the opening must hook the persona, agitate the problem, and introduce the mechanism before the product.
cards.use_when: Scripting the opening of a long-form VSL used on a landing page or as a paid social placement.
steps: Open with a persona call-out, ideally covering multiple related personas to widen the top of funnel.
Move into problem agitation: what the viewer has tried, why it failed, and what their doctor or previous solutions did not address.
Introduce the mechanism or reframe the cause before naming the product — the IM8 example goes from gut problems to bacteria balance before the product.
Continue the education into the product's mechanism (prebiotics, postbiotics, how probiotics colonize) before bridging to the offer.
Stack credibility next: clinical trial percentages, nutrient counts and multiple reported benefits, then close.
The source also suggests keeping the middle flowing and not making the bridge into the product too aggressive.
caveats: The 3-4 minute length is described as typical, not mandatory.
Trial and nutrient figures are the brand's claims from the example ad.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Build a swipe file of competitor ad libraries for creative research
cards.summary: Watch the ad libraries of brands whose creatives are performing to study execution patterns you can adapt.
cards.use_when: Sourcing new ad angles, hooks or formats for your store's paid social creative pipeline.
steps: Identify brands consistently shipping strong direct-response creatives in your category — the source names IM8 as one to watch.
Study hook mechanics, bridge construction, editing density and problem agitation in their ads rather than just the products advertised.
Note how long each ad has been running and its visible engagement as rough signals of whether it is working.
Adapt the structural pattern to your own product; do not copy claims or product efficacy commentary.
Use findings to brief new scripts and edits rather than as finished creative.
caveats: Engagement counts and run time are weak proxies; the source uses 'three likes over a couple of weeks' as an informal signal, not a measurement system.
The source notes ad performance metrics, ROAS, scaling and attribution belong in a separate domain, not creative analysis.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Diagnose underperformance by segmenting hook, bridge and body
cards.summary: When an ad underperforms, review the hook, the bridge and the body separately to locate the failure point.
cards.use_when: Troubleshooting a video ad that has low conversion or low engagement after launch.
steps: Watch the ad in three segments: hook (first 3-5 seconds), body education, and the bridge between them.
Score the hook: does it qualify the right persona, or just grab attention?
Score the bridge: does it introduce the product too early or too aggressively?
Score the body: does it educate, handle objections and translate features into benefits?

Connect the diagnosis to the specific segment rather than rewriting the whole ad. In the FU2 example, the source says the hook and early education were strong and suspects the aggressive bridge caused the underperformance.
Keep the strongest segment and test a revised version of the weakest.
caveats: The FU2 attribution to the bridge is the presenter's inference from low engagement over a couple of weeks, not a controlled test.
One ad's run time or like count is not a reliable performance metric.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Adapt hooks and education to the audience's awareness stage
cards.summary: The same product can be advertised at different awareness stages, but the level of education must match what the viewer already knows.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether a given ad should target problem-aware or solution-aware audiences in a Meta campaign.
steps: Classify the ad's implied audience stage by how much the body explains.
Problem-aware audiences need education on what the mechanism is and why it declines — the source says the NAD ad under-explains what NAD is and why it drops.
Solution-aware audiences already know the mechanism; they need reinforcement, differentiation and the offer.
If the audience is problem-aware, add the missing 'why' before the pitch or expect the ad to underperform with that group.
Use the stage classification to decide campaign placement rather than forcing one ad to serve every stage.
caveats: Stage labels are the source's analytical framing, not measured segments.
The source's assessment of which stage an ad fits is interpretive.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx

cards.title: Meet the numbers you promise in ad claims and copy
cards.summary: Ad claims like 'clinical study' figures or 'up to X% off' must be accurate and verifiable or they damage credibility with engaged viewers.
cards.use_when: Finalizing claims, offers and supporting numbers for a video ad or product page.
steps: Check every numeric claim in the script against a source you can defend — the examples include '82% of users' from a clinical study and 'up to 16% off.'
Keep offer claims simple and specific; the shaker ad's 'up to 16% off today' is a dated offer that needs correct dates and terms.
If you cite a trial, state what it measured; the IM8 ad reports 85% better digestion, 95% more energy, 80% better sleep.
Remove unsupported disease or efficacy claims unless they are clearly compliant in your market.
Review the final script against the product page so the offer the ad promises is redeemable at checkout.
caveats: All figures above come from the example ads and are the brands' claims, not verified results or benchmarks.
The source explicitly admits uncertainty about compliance on some claims.
cards.source_name: How To Make A Winner Meta Video Ad.docx
